breadcrumb.name: Challenges of International Business in 2026 & How to Overcome Them

contentHtml:
Expanding a business internationally opens doors to new opportunities. However, it also comes with significant obstacles. While global markets offer growth potential, companies often face:

  • Compliance issues
  • Workforce challenges
  • Taxation complexities
  • Operational inefficiencies 

To succeed, businesses must first understand these challenges of international business. Then, they need to apply strategies to reduce risks and ensure a smooth expansion.

Many companies struggle with problems of international business, including complex legal frameworks, payroll processing struggles, talent acquisition difficulties, and business setup roadblocks. Below, we break down these real-world international business issues and explore potential solutions to simplify global expansion.

Top Challenges Businesses Face When Expanding Internationally

1. Compliance with Local Employment & Tax Laws

Navigating employment and tax laws in a foreign country isn’t just about filling out forms. It’s about understanding how things actually work. Every country has its own tax rules, employee benefits, and labor laws. Businesses need to follow these to stay compliant.

Expanding globally? That means dealing with payroll taxes, social security contributions, and corporate tax policies. These can be completely different from one country to another. Even a small mistake can lead to massive fines. In the worst case, it could even shut down a business. Some countries, like Saudi Arabia, have particularly strict labor laws.

Take Saudization (Nitaqat) in Saudi, for example. Companies must hire a certain percentage of local employees. If they don’t, they risk fines and work permit restrictions. In some cases, their business operations could be suspended. Staying compliant isn’t just a formality—it’s what keeps businesses running smoothly.

✔ Real-world Issue: Companies misinterpret tax structures, struggle with documentation, and violate contract rules. This leads to penalties and legal trouble..

✔ Why It Matters: Local laws evolve frequently, and businesses must stay updated to avoid disruptions.

2. Complex Payroll Processing & Multi-Currency Payments

Handling payroll across different countries isn’t simple—it involves multiple tax regulations, social security contributions, exchange rates, and reporting mandates. Each country has unique payroll laws. Businesses must adapt to different tax brackets, social security percentages, and statutory benefits.

In Saudi Arabia, companies must comply with the Wage Protection System (WPS)—salaries must be processed through an approved payment structure. Non-compliance can lead to penalties, payment blocks, or even work permit suspensions.

Additionally, businesses must align payroll with GOSI (General Organization for Social Insurance) contributions. They need to ensure the correct percentages are deducted for both Saudi nationals and expatriates.

✔ Real-world Issue: Many businesses struggle with payroll miscalculations due to complex tax laws and varying contributions. This leads to financial penalties, delayed salaries, and unhappy employees.

✔ Why It Matters: Payroll errors affect employee retention, compliance, and business reputation. Accurate payroll ensures legal adherence, workforce stability, and smooth international expansion.

3. Recruiting & Managing a Global Workforce

Talent acquisition is one of the biggest hurdles in global expansion. Businesses must comply with local hiring laws, offer competitive salaries, and manage remote teams effectively. Each country has different labor policies—some impose strict employment quotas, while others require specific work permits and visas.

In Saudi Arabia, hiring involves navigating the Kafala system (visa sponsorship). This system governs expatriate employment and work permits. Employers must sponsor foreign workers and comply with regulations on work permits, labor contracts, and end-of-service benefits.

Any violations can lead to hefty fines or visa restrictions. To avoid this, businesses must align their hiring practices with legal requirements.

✔ Real-world Issue: Companies struggle to attract skilled professionals due to inadequate market knowledge and slow hiring processes. Complex visa regulations make it even more challenging.

✔ Why It Matters: Mismanaged recruitment leads to high turnover rates and employee dissatisfaction. In industries reliant on expatriate talent, it can also cause major operational disruptions.

4. Business Setup & Market Entry Barriers

Starting operations in a foreign market requires extensive paperwork, licenses, work permits, and compliance with banking regulations. Any delays in legal approvals can halt business operations for months.

Foreign businesses entering Saudi Arabia must follow SAGIA (Saudi Arabian General Investment Authority) regulations. These rules govern foreign ownership and licensing requirements.

✔ Real-world Issue: Bureaucratic hurdles slow down company registration and legal entity setup, delaying time to market.

✔ Why It Matters: A delayed entry into a new market can mean lost business opportunities and increased setup costs.

5. Economic Instability & Currency Risks

International markets are volatile. Fluctuations in exchange rates, inflation, and government policies impact pricing and financial planning. Although the Saudi Riyal is pegged to the U.S. dollar, businesses must still account for inflation and the economic impact of oil price fluctuations.

✔ Real-world Issue: Businesses frequently suffer unexpected losses due to poor currency risk management.

✔ Why It Matters: Managing financial stability is critical for sustaining global operations.

6. Supply Chain Disruptions

Global supply chains involve logistics, customs duties, import/export regulations, and supplier relationships. Any disruption can significantly affect operations. Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 focuses on boosting local manufacturing and reducing import dependency. However, businesses must adapt to evolving trade policies and customs regulations.

✔ Real-world Issue: Companies face unexpected delays and rising costs due to geopolitical issues. Changing import/export laws add to the challenge.

✔ Why It Matters: Poor supply chain management leads to reputational damage. It also creates serious operational inefficiencies.

Strategies to Overcome International Business Challenges

Challenge How to Resolve It
Compliance with Local Laws Partner with legal consultants or an Employer of Record (EOR) to manage compliance and reduce legal risks.
Payroll Processing & Multi-Currency Payments Outsource payroll processing to ensure compliance with local tax laws and accurate salary disbursement.
Global Talent Acquisition & Management Use international recruitment services to find, hire, and onboard top talent efficiently.
Business Setup & Expansion Delays Utilize business setup services to navigate bureaucratic procedures, obtain licenses, and establish banking structures quickly.
Economic & Currency Risks Implement financial hedging strategies and work with global payroll providers to stabilize payments.
Supply Chain Management Develop contingency plans, diversify suppliers, and stay informed on global trade policies.

Navigating the Future

The global marketplace offers immense growth potential. However, businesses must navigate complexities of international business, including legal, financial, and operational challenges, to succeed.

Expanding internationally is challenging. But with the right strategies, companies can avoid costly mistakes and build a strong global presence.

By implementing effective compliance frameworks and outsourcing key functions, businesses can simplify international expansion. Staying informed on regulatory changes also helps minimize risks.

A proactive approach to problems of international business is the key to long-term success.
